oneSentence: A formally counted vote where each participant’s position is entered into the official record, often by name, so others can see who supported, opposed or abstained.
plainExplanation:
A recorded vote is a formal way to show how a group reached a result. Instead of only announcing that a proposal passed or failed, the meeting record also shows how each participant voted. In many UN settings, that means listing which Member States voted in favour, against, or abstained.

What goes in is a draft text or proposal, plus the members entitled to vote. What happens is that the chair calls for voting and the secretariat or another authorised office counts and records each vote. An abstention means a participant is present but chooses not to vote either for or against.

What comes out is both a final outcome and a public record of positions. For example, the result may say that a resolution was adopted by 120 in favour, 12 against and 25 abstentions, with the country names listed in the official meeting record.

This is different from consensus. Consensus usually means the chair finds there is no stated objection, so there may be no formal count of each vote. A recorded vote is also different from informal polling, which can test opinion without creating an official record.

everydayAnalogy.title: A school council vote with names on the board
everydayAnalogy.story: A school council in Nairobi, Lima and Bangkok is meeting online to choose one of three projects for a shared exchange programme. Instead of asking for a quick show of hands, the facilitator calls each school in turn and writes its choice on a visible board: Project A, Project B, or abstain. At the end, everyone can see both the total numbers and which school took which position. If someone later asks how the decision was made, the board provides the record.

everydayAnalogy.limitation: The analogy is simpler than real UN practice. In UN bodies, voting rights, quorum, rules of procedure, and the legal effect of the result matter, and the official record may appear in several documents rather than on one board. Also, not every UN body votes in exactly the same way, and some decisions are adopted without a recorded vote at all.

visual.title: How a recorded vote becomes an official result
visual.learningObjective: After viewing this, a reader should be able to explain how a proposal turns into both a counted outcome and a named record of positions.
visual.description: A left-to-right step diagram with four boxes. It starts with a draft proposal, then shows the call for votes, then the recording of each participant’s position, and ends with the published result. Read from first box to last to see how the process creates both totals and an official record.

steps.label: 1. Proposal on the floor
steps.explanation: A draft resolution, amendment or other proposal is formally put before the meeting for a decision.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a document icon labelled 'Draft text' entering the first box. Add a small caption: 'Item ready for decision'.

steps.label: 2. Chair calls the vote
steps.explanation: The presiding officer opens voting under the body’s rules and asks eligible members to cast their positions.
steps.visualInstruction: Show a simple chairperson icon with three outgoing labels: 'in favour', 'against', 'abstain'.

steps.label: 3. Votes are counted and recorded
steps.explanation: An authorised office records how each member voted and totals the numbers in each category.
steps.visualInstruction: Display a grid of member labels with one marked in each of three colours or patterns for the three vote types, plus counters for totals.

steps.label: 4. Official result is issued
steps.explanation: The meeting announces whether the proposal was adopted or rejected, and the record shows the named positions where applicable.
steps.visualInstruction: Show an output panel with 'Adopted' or 'Rejected' above a summary line such as '120-12-25' and a note 'positions entered in record'.

visual.interaction: On hover or tap, each step reveals a short example line from a fictional meeting record showing how totals and named votes appear together.
visual.accessibilityDescription: This diagram explains a recorded vote as a four-step process. First, a draft proposal is formally placed before a meeting. Second, the chair opens voting and asks eligible members to vote in favour, against, or abstain. Third, an authorised office records each member’s position and counts the totals in each category. Fourth, the meeting announces the outcome, such as adopted or rejected, and the official record shows both the totals and, where the rules provide, the named positions of members. The main idea is that a recorded vote produces two outputs: a decision and a traceable record of how participants voted.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: A static four-box sequence shows the same process without animation: proposal, call for vote, recording and counting, then official result with totals and named positions.

workedExample.scenario: In a fictional UN committee, 30 Member States vote on a draft resolution about sharing good practices for AI literacy in public services.
process: The chair announces that the committee will take a recorded vote on draft L.18.
Each Member State votes 'in favour', 'against' or 'abstain', and the secretariat logs each position.
The totals are counted: 22 in favour, 3 against, 5 abstentions.
The chair announces that the draft is adopted, and the meeting record lists the voting figures and the names under each category.
workedExample.result: The proposal passes, and anyone reading the official record can see both the final numbers and which Member States took each position.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: A UN staff member preparing a briefing note for delegates reviews an official meeting record to confirm whether an AI-related resolution was adopted by consensus or by a recorded vote, and to note the voting pattern accurately.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: This matters because the method of adoption can affect how observers interpret the level of support, the positions of Member States, and the political context around an AI governance text.

whyItMatters: For non-specialists, a recorded vote is one of the clearest ways to see how a formal decision was made. It shows not only the result but also the pattern of support, opposition and abstention. That can help you read political signals more carefully. A text adopted without a vote may suggest broad acceptance, while a recorded vote may show visible disagreement even if the text still passes. In AI governance, that distinction matters because rules, principles and resolutions often gain meaning from who backed them, who objected, and how divided the room was.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A recorded vote means the proposal was controversial.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Not always. Some proposals are put to a recorded vote for procedural, political or transparency reasons even when the result is not close. The record shows positions, but it does not by itself explain why voting was requested.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If there is no recorded vote, nobody knows what happened.
commonMisconceptions.correction: The outcome can still be official without a recorded vote. For example, a text may be adopted by consensus or another procedure under the body’s rules. The difference is that there may be no formal name-by-name voting list.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Abstaining means the same as voting against.
commonMisconceptions.correction: An abstention is a separate position. It shows that a participant did not support the text, but also did not oppose it formally. In practice, that can signal caution, mixed views or procedural reasons.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: It is a formal vote that leaves a trace. You do not only learn whether something passed. You also learn how each participant voted, or at least that their positions were officially counted and entered into the record.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: In UN and similar intergovernmental settings, a recorded vote is a decision-making procedure in which the votes of eligible members are individually cast, counted and entered into the official record in accordance with the body’s rules of procedure. The output usually includes totals for votes in favour, against and abstentions, and may also list Member States under each category in meeting records or related documentation. This should be distinguished from adoption by consensus, where the chair determines that there is no expressed objection and no formal tally is taken, and from informal soundings that test support without producing an official vote record. Exact practice can vary by organ, agenda item and applicable rules.

keyTakeaway: A recorded vote does two things at once: it decides the issue and creates an official trace of who stood where.

quickCheck.question: What makes a recorded vote different from adoption by consensus?
options: It produces an official count and record of positions rather than only noting no objection.
It always means every participant supports the proposal.
It is used only in Security Council meetings.
It prevents abstentions from being counted.
quickCheck.explanation: A recorded vote creates a formal tally and record of how participants voted. By contrast, consensus usually means the chair notes that no one objected, without taking a formal counted vote. Recorded votes can happen in different UN bodies, and abstentions are normally counted as a separate category.
